situation: You are the one who always proposes plans. Time together is warm, but when you stop texting, contact stops. What you know: the pattern and how the meetings feel. What you don't know: why your friend doesn't initiate (busyness, habit, shyness, a different style, or lower interest) and whether they would want to hear that you've noticed. That unknown decides whether speaking up is a request, a test, or a risk. (This is a fictional discussion to help you think, not a verdict on your friend.)

minds.title: The Friendship Realist
minds.concern: What kind of friendship this is, and whether the effort on each side is in balance and mutual goodwill
minds.author: Aristotle

minds.title: The Conversation Mapper
minds.concern: How to raise a sensitive topic without accusing, by separating what happened from the stories we attach to it
minds.author: Douglas Stone, Bruce Patton and Sheila Heen

minds.title: The Bid Watcher
minds.concern: The small everyday reaches for connection, and the different ways people make and miss them
minds.author: John Gottman

debate.speaker: The Friendship Realist
debate.text: Start with the evidence: you plan, they enjoy it, and silence follows when you stop. Friendships built on pleasure can be real but thin. If only one person ever moves the friendship forward, it may be a pleasant acquaintance wearing a friend's coat. I'd test that before investing more.
debate.author: Aristotle
debate.basis: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, on kinds of friendship (books VIII-IX); source not verified, paraphrase only.

debate.speaker: The Bid Watcher
debate.text: That's a big verdict from one pattern. Maybe they show interest in ways you don't count. Do they reply warmly, remember your news, say yes fast? Some people reach out rarely but respond reliably. Counting only who texts first can make a loving friend look indifferent.
debate.author: John Gottman
debate.basis: Gottman, The Relationship Cure, on bids for connection; source not verified, paraphrase only.

debate.speaker: The Friendship Realist
debate.text: Fair, responsiveness counts. But reliable replies to your reaches are not the same as reaching. I'd go further than Aristotle here: if you never test the pattern, you're guessing. The cheap test is going quiet for a while, though it has a cost, and you'd be the one paying it.
debate.author: Aristotle
debate.basis: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, on reciprocity in friendship; source not verified, paraphrase only. The extension about testing is the speaker's own.

debate.speaker: The Conversation Mapper
debate.text: Going quiet is a silent experiment, and silence gets read through whatever story the other person already holds. They might think you're busy, or hurt, or done. You'd also be judging the result through your own story. Why not separate the facts from the stories and say the facts aloud?
debate.author: Douglas Stone, Bruce Patton and Sheila Heen
debate.basis: Stone, Patton and Heen, Difficult Conversations, on separating the what-happened conversation from the story we tell about it; source not verified, paraphrase only.

debate.speaker: The Bid Watcher
debate.text: But even a gentle talk can land as a complaint about their character. If they are a low-initiator by temperament, 'you never text first' feels like a failing they can't fix. A specific, small ask like 'I'd love it if you picked the next one' is easier to answer than a pattern review.
debate.author: John Gottman
debate.basis: Gottman, The Relationship Cure, on how bids are made and received; source not verified, paraphrase only. Application to low-initiators is the speaker's own.

debate.speaker: The Conversation Mapper
debate.text: I'll concede that, and it narrows my point. Don't announce a verdict about them. Describe your side: you've noticed you do most of the planning, you enjoy them, and you'd like to know how they see it. Curiosity about their view keeps the door open to reasons I can't see.
debate.author: Douglas Stone, Bruce Patton and Sheila Heen
debate.basis: Stone, Patton and Heen, Difficult Conversations, on entering with curiosity and contributing your own part; source not verified, paraphrase only.

debate.speaker: The Friendship Realist
debate.text: Curiosity is fine, but watch the motive. If you speak mainly hoping they'll start texting, you've made it a demand wearing a question. Ask yourself first whether you'd still want this friendship if they said, kindly, that they'd always be a replier. Some friendships are worth keeping on those terms, and some aren't.
debate.author: Aristotle
debate.basis: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, on friendship valued for itself versus for what it yields (books VIII-IX); source not verified, paraphrase only. The application is the speaker's own.

debate.speaker: The Bid Watcher
debate.text: Then there's the doing-less option, which deserves a fair hearing. You could simply keep planning, because the meetings are lovely and the cost may be small. Resentment is what turns a lopsided habit into a problem, so the real question is whether you feel it yet or only expect to.
debate.author: John Gottman
debate.basis: Gottman, The Relationship Cure, on small daily connection and the build-up of unmet needs; source not verified, paraphrase only. The wait-and-see framing is the speaker's own.

debate.speaker: The Conversation Mapper
debate.text: That's the hinge. If you feel no sting, saying something may just invent a problem. If you notice a tightening each time you open your phone, silence is also a message you're sending to yourself. In that case I'd speak sooner, and in person or on a call, not by text.
debate.author: Douglas Stone, Bruce Patton and Sheila Heen
debate.basis: Stone, Patton and Heen, Difficult Conversations, on the feelings conversation and what unspoken feelings do; source not verified, paraphrase only.

debate.speaker: The Friendship Realist
debate.text: I'll soften my first claim. One lopsided pattern doesn't prove a thin friendship. But I still hold that a friendship where only one person moves is worth examining, and I'd count their response to a direct, kind ask as better evidence than any amount of guessing.
debate.author: Aristotle
debate.basis: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, on mutual goodwill being recognized by both friends (book VIII); source not verified, paraphrase only.

debate.speaker: The Bid Watcher
debate.text: And I'd add one practical step: give them a chance to bid before you ask. Mention something small, like wanting to see a film, and leave it open for a week. If they pick it up, that's information too, and it costs neither of you a hard conversation.
debate.author: John Gottman
debate.basis: Gottman, The Relationship Cure, on noticing and turning toward bids; source not verified, paraphrase only. The one-week experiment is the speaker's own.

clearer: The main insight is that there are two separate questions: what the pattern means about your friend, and what it is doing to you. The first can't be settled from the outside; the second you can check yourself. Still disputed: whether quietly testing the pattern is wiser than a direct, curious conversation, and how much a rare initiator should be read as lower interest. A possible self-reflection: if your friend said they'd always be the one who replies, would that feel like enough?
dependsOn: If you feel no resentment and the meetings are reliably warm, continuing as you are is reasonable, because the cost is small and speaking could create a problem that isn't there. If you notice resentment, or find yourself keeping score, a short, specific, non-accusing conversation becomes more reasonable, because the feeling will otherwise leak out anyway. If you are unsure why they don't initiate, a low-cost way to learn is to leave a casual opening for a week or two and see whether they take it, then ask kindly how they see your roles. If they respond with care and change little, you can decide whether you want a replier-style friend. If they respond defensively or not at all, the friendship may be thinner than the meetings suggest, and your effort can go elsewhere.
